intro: Chaliapin’s 1927 remake pairs the same Pushkin setting with Albert Coates’s orchestral accompaniment. The source documents a 1928 release; recording rights are territorial European public domain, with US status unestablished.
question: What changes when the same singer returns to the same text?

cues.title: The same singer returns
cues.text: Chaliapin sings the same Pushkin setting six years after the acoustic side, now with Albert Coates. Follow the length of his phrases rather than deciding that a different recorded balance must mean a different vocal technique.
cues.evidence: The source names Chaliapin, Coates and 20 October 1927: https://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Gramophone-db1103-2-022043. The discography distinguishes this take 2 from the June 1927 take 1.

cues.title: Carry the line onwards
cues.text: Through this opening span, attend to how a held vowel leads into the next syllable. Compare that connection with 1921; neither the automatic map nor the level trace identifies individual sung words.
cues.evidence: The report places this after the measured 0:30 change, in a continuous opening span. The suggestion concerns phrasing, not a timestamped word or breath.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The early crest expands
cues.text: This passage grows into a sustained high-level span before withdrawing. Listen to the time spent across the crest, not merely its peak: a phrase can broaden without a new musical idea appearing.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-prophet-chaliapin-1927.txt: relative level rises at 1:30 and remains near −7 to −8 dB at 1:35–1:45, then drops by 1:50. No bar or word is assigned.

cues.title: A longer quiet space
cues.text: The middle stretch lowers the recorded level before a fresh rise. In the side-by-side comparison, follow the time between the preceding crest and the renewed pressure rather than using the two files’ total lengths as a tempo reading.
cues.evidence: The report shows −28.3 to −25.4 dB at 2:10–2:25 and a marked rise at 2:30. This is a measured passage, not an identified vocal pause.

cues.title: Pressure gathers again
cues.text: The low-level span gives way to a more sustained presence. Keep following the line across the changing accompaniment, rather than treating every fluctuation in the transfer as a separate expressive accent.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest novelty peak is 2:32; relative level rises sharply between 2:25 and 2:35. The analysis does not separate singer and orchestra.

cues.title: The late quiet passage
cues.text: A further withdrawal separates this stretch from the final crest. The automatic match is less certain here, so listen for the larger phrase rather than expecting the switch to land on precisely the same syllable.
cues.evidence: The report gives −27.6 dB at 3:15, followed by rebuilding. The map’s three points below 0.8 confidence fall at approximately 3:19–3:20 in this recording.

cues.title: Holding the final crest
cues.text: The last large span maintains a high recorded level. Compare how the bass sustains its line over the accompaniment with the earlier side; the relative-level trace cannot measure how loudly either singer performed in the studio.
cues.evidence: The report identifies 3:40 and 4:05 among the loudest windows, with high relative level between them. This comparison stays within the transfer’s measured envelope.

cues.title: Release and residual sound
cues.text: The ending withdraws from that sustained crest. Listen past the last strong sound into the remaining resonance and disc noise; the comparison stops before the quiet tail rather than matching noise as music.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −8.4 dB at 4:10 to −13.9 at 4:15 and −37.6 at 4:20. The alignment input ends at 259 seconds; no exact release is claimed.

facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
